questions.q: What kind of problem does IaC scanning catch that SAST and SCA do not?
options: Vulnerabilities in open-source dependencies
Misconfigurations baked directly into infrastructure definitions, like a storage resource left open to public access
SQL injection patterns in application code
Secrets accidentally committed to git history
questions.explain: SAST analyzes application code and SCA analyzes dependencies — neither reads Terraform, ARM, Bicep, or Kubernetes manifests, so neither can catch an infrastructure misconfiguration.

questions.q: In the example Checkov finding, what does the check ID CKV_AZURE_59 identify?
options: The specific rule that failed, independent of which resource triggered it
The CVE number of a vulnerable dependency
A random tracking number with no fixed meaning
The Terraform provider version in use
questions.explain: The check ID identifies exactly which configuration rule failed — in this case, a rule requiring storage accounts to disallow public access — regardless of which specific resource triggered it.

questions.q: Why should IaC scanning run against the Terraform plan in CI, rather than only checking already-deployed infrastructure?
options: Because checking deployed infrastructure is technically impossible
Because catching the misconfiguration before apply means the resource is never actually provisioned in a vulnerable state
Because CI pipelines cannot run any kind of scan
Because Terraform plans are always smaller than deployed infrastructure
questions.explain: Scanning at plan time, before apply, prevents the misconfigured resource from ever existing in the real environment — catching it after deployment means it was already live and exposed.

questions.q: Which of these is a tool built specifically for infrastructure-as-code scanning?
options: Dependabot
CodeQL
Checkov
Falco
questions.explain: Checkov (along with tools like tfsec and Terrascan) is purpose-built to parse infrastructure-as-code files and check them against known misconfiguration patterns.

questions.q: In the lesson's Northbridge Retail example, what was the actual misconfiguration found?
options: A hardcoded database password in a Python script
A storage account for product catalog images left without restricted public access
A critical CVE in a logging library
A missing required reviewer on a deployment environment
questions.explain: The example involved a Terraform-defined storage account for product images that was left open to public access — a configuration issue caught by Checkov before it reached production.
